case_name: State of Bihar v Madan Mohan Prasad and Others
facts: Respondents 1, 2 and 3 made an application under Article 226 of the Constitution alleging that the decision of the Bihar State Government fixing the seniority of Respondent 4 below Shri C. P. Singh (Respondent 5) and Shri E. Rehman (Respondent 6) was illegal and ultra vires.

The applicants also challenged the upgrading of the posts of Deputy Registrar, Patna High Court and the Secretary, Bihar Legislative Assembly with effect from June 17, 1959 till the posts were held by Respondents 5 and 6, respectively.
Prior to that date, four posts of Additional District and Sessions Judges fell vacant.
On April 25, 1959, the High Court recommended Respondents 4, 5 and 6 and Shri Sharda Prasad for promotion as Additional District & Sessions Judges in those vacancies.
Respondent 4 was recommended to be promoted as Additional District & Sessions Judge in the third longer vacancy.
He joined in the promoted rank on June 17, 1959 and continued in it till October 1, 1959.

On August 5, 1959, the Government by its letter had approved the creation of two posts of Additional District and Sessions Judges for a period of one year in the first instance, consequent on the amendment of Bengal, Agra and Assam Civil Court Act, 1887.
On May 22, 1959, the Government sanctioned the creation of two posts of Peripatetic District & Sessions Judges for a period of two years.
issues: The interpretation of Rule 16(e) of the Bihar Superior Judicial Service Rules
Whether the power to determine seniority vests exclusively with the High Court under Article 235 of the Constitution
petitioner_arguments: The contention that the expression 'may have been allowed to officiate continuously' in Rule 16(e) means actual and continuous officiation, not a fictional or notional one.

The argument that the Government could not fix the seniority of Respondent 4 as they had done by taking recourse to the 'hardship rule' framed by them under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The contention that the expression 'may have been allowed to officiate continuously' in Rule 16(e) means notional, continuous officiation, and that a promoted officer should be given preference over a direct recruit in the matter of seniority.
The argument that the Government had the power to determine seniority under Article 235 of the Constitution.
court_reasoning: The High Court rejected the contention that the expression 'may have been allowed to officiate continuously' means notional, continuous officiation and held that it means actual and continuous officiation.
The High Court held that the power to determine seniority vests exclusively with the High Court under Article 235 of the Constitution.
holding: The Government's decision to fix Respondent 4's seniority was upheld.
The matter has been rendered academic, except for the limited purpose of fixing pension and gratuity on the basis of the length of service in the cadre of Superior Judicial Service.
